P1.evidence: Setter notes referenced ('I already heard a few things from Kim'), and a nice extra touch in asking how to pronounce his name before starting. Frame is the same three-part version — where you're at, where you want to go, whether we fit — still missing what's in the way and what you need. Agreement asked and given, open question ran verbatim.

P2.evidence: The most complete baseline in the batch. Weight was asked properly ('whereabouts are you at with weights when it comes to physique?') and produced the 30-40 lb gap and the 185 target, though height was never asked and current weight never actually stated. The injury probe was excellent — 'is it knees, shoulders, what things come up?' followed by the 1-to-10 severity scale, surfacing the herniated disc and a 6/10. Health went deeper than any other call here: the doctor's six-month ultimatum, fluctuating blood pressure, and the hereditary thread through his father's medication. Diet was probed to specifics including frequency ('every few days') and the structural cause (hotels without kitchens). Energy was asked directly and answered 'Low'. Sleep was engaged with via the rotating shift pattern but never asked about as quantity or quality. Work is the soft spot — the rep learned he travels and works midnights but never established what he actually does, which matters for the ICP.

P3.evidence: Textbook, and the best example in the batch of the phase doing its job. The physical-thing-you-cannot-do-now check landed early via the Spartan races — 'at the moment it sounds like you don't really have that option, you can be like, oh, I can jump into that race tomorrow.' The bridge ran twice and produced the doctor's ultimatum, then the rep pushed past it: 'a lot of people are like, I'm 56, it's okay, I'll just accept it. Why are you like, no, I need to take matters into my own hands?' That question produced the whole emotional core — the four-year-old granddaughter's high school graduation thirteen years out, the eight-year-old's wedding, and the great-grandparent legacy modelled on his own parents. He then ran the future-pace twice, on the doctor's office and on the graduation, and closed with a clean reflect-back that named the real driver: 'Sounds like that's the actual reason for why you want to put in all of the efforts.' Only P3f is soft — the impact on others emerged from the why question rather than from being asked directly.

P4.evidence: The blocker question ran and did the heavy lifting: 'What do you feel like you would need in order to actually be able to stick to that?' produced the single most useful line on the call — 'I know what to do. I just have no accountability' — which is the gap named in the prospect's own words, exactly what P4e asks for. Past attempts were only lightly covered: the rep asked how long he had been searching and got the travel-and-weight-gain story, but never asked what he had tried, what happened with it, or why it did not stick. P4f was never posed as a question; the answer arrived anyway because the P4d probe was well aimed.

P5.evidence: The consequence question ran with a concrete horizon and a concrete scene: 'if you don't make a change and it keeps on going the same way, and in six months you go to the doctors and they tell you, Jeffrey, it's not a good place, it's all in the same position. How would you feel about that?' The problem is what came back — the prospect refused the frame entirely ('I don't think negative. I think positive, accentuate the positivities') and talked for two minutes about his own drive instead. The rep did not re-land it; he explained why he had asked and moved on, then asserted rather than asked the settle question: 'it sounds like you're not willing to settle for the dosage.' The line in the sand did run cleanly — 'Ready for also putting in that effort, the time, and the energy to fixing that now instead of waiting?' — and got a firm yes. Net: the phase was attempted properly and deflected, and the deflection was accepted.

P6.evidence: The best sequencing discipline in the batch. When the prospect asked for the price mid-presentation the rep held it back and ran the belief check first: 'Before I go into that, do you feel like, yes, this is something I see myself doing, because otherwise the price really doesn't matter?' — answered 'Yes, yes, yes, yes, yes.' Commitment had also been tested before the presentation ('if you're willing to give up, then don't even start. But you have that commitment... I don't know if you agree with that?'). The composite go-all-in question was never asked as such; the rep relied on per-pillar confirmations instead.

P11.evidence: No agreement and no deposit, so nothing downstream was reachable. The rep did secure a dated follow-up with the invite confirmed live, which is the correct fallback.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in the batch. Isolation ran and got a clean answer — 'outside of the investment, do you feel like, yeah, let's just get started?' / 'I could get started outside of the investment, yes'. Then the financial picture, most of it: leftover each month after bills ($1,500), cash set aside ($2,000-2,500 liquid), credit score (self-described poor), number of credit cards (four), debt carried (about $3,000) and available credit ($300-500/month). The instalment option was offered rather than waited for. Two gaps. The last scripted item — crypto, stocks, investments — was skipped even though the prospect handed it over unprompted, mentioning a Roth account and stock investments he had not recently valued; that is where $6,000 most plausibly lives and it was never opened. And the rep did not use the 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place' reframe, which was available and would have fitted, since the prospect had already conceded he wanted to start.

'I would like to sit down for a day or two and budget everything' at 00:34:51. Several moves ran in substance: the direct feasibility test ('do you feel like $6,000 at the moment is feasible for you?' — answered 'Yeah, I can do that'), the challenge ('is that just a no right now because you really want to look at it, or is it just that uncertainty?'), and a strong pattern-interrupt on what happens after the call ends. Missing the sharpest moves — 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here, when do you make a different decision', and 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now'. That last one was gift-wrapped: the prospect had just quoted Rocky, 'there is no tomorrow', unprompted. The rep echoed the quote twice but never turned it into the decision. Instead he substituted the deposit device.

Timing surfaced in substance — 'that's kind of steep right now with my inconsistent working' and the risk of the assignment ending that night. The rep ran the core OD insight, that waiting becomes never: 'when you go off the meeting, it's like, well, maybe it's not the best time right now. And it gets pushed forward. That is what happens a lot.' None of the harder moves ran — nothing on things never slowing down, nothing on the cost of delay compounding, and notably nothing on the one lever that was sitting there: a doctor has given him six months, so the deadline is external and real. 'The longer you wait the harder this gets' had a literal clinical form on this call and went unused.

The rep probed for it — 'it could be that it's maybe a little bit of uncertainty around making the decision' — and was told directly it was not: 'the uncertainty is just financing the decision.' Correctly did not force the play. He did normalise the discomfort well ('if it wouldn't be somewhat of an uncertain decision, then it probably also wouldn't have been the best decision').
No partner or spouse in the decision; he appears to be deciding alone.

Script gap: genuinely irregular income. This is not the same objection as 'I can't afford it' — he can afford $1,200 in a good month and cannot in a month with no assignment, and he does not know which this is until tonight. OC assumes a stable picture you can total up; there is no play for volatile contract income, no concept of pausing or deferring a payment when work stops, and no scripted way to structure around it. The rep's instinct was right, offering instalments to avoid draining his $2,500 cushion, but $1,200 a month against a $1,500 surplus that may vanish is not obviously safe and was never stress-tested.

Second gap: an unpriced commitment device. The rep introduced a refundable $100 deposit as an accountability mechanism rather than as a payment — 'it's not like we need it, it's more so for yourself to actually already make a step'. That is nowhere in the playbook and it was paired with a scarcity claim that was immediately contradicted: 'usually we don't really book in another meeting... unless we actually have a deposit', followed by booking the meeting with no deposit. Either the deposit is a policy and should be scripted, or it is not and should not be implied as one.

notes: Richard's best call in this batch on process: full baseline, the emotional why driven all the way to a four-year-old granddaughter's graduation, price withheld until he had a yes, and a genuinely thorough money conversation. Three things cost him the close on the day. He let the consequence frame be deflected — the prospect answered 'I don't think negative' and the rep accepted it, losing the urgency a doctor's six-month ultimatum had already handed him. He skipped the investments question after the prospect volunteered a Roth and a stock portfolio. And the instalment maths went out wrong: $1,200 x 6 is $7,200 against a $6,000 headline, while the prospect said aloud 'that's only a thousand a month' and was not corrected. Fix the number before tomorrow's call, open the investment accounts, and use the doctor's deadline as the close.
